q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE reform undertaken by the Meiji government to modernize Japan.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why Japan's response to Western pressure differed from China's response in the nineteenth century, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which Meiji modernization continued traditional Japanese social hierarchies.

sample_answers.a: The Meiji government abolished the feudal domains and the samurai class, replacing them with a centralized bureaucracy, a conscript army, and a national education system modeled on Western lines.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, Japan's relatively compact size and the Meiji leaders' ability to seize the central state let them impose reform from above, while China's vast bureaucracy and the Qing court's resistance to change blocked similar efforts by reformers.
sample_answers.c: Although the samurai class was formally abolished, former samurai dominated the new army officer corps, bureaucracy, and business elite, so the old warrior aristocracy largely reinvented itself as Japan's modern ruling class.

q1.stimulus:
Historians often present Meiji Japan as the great success story of defensive modernization — the one non-Western society that industrialized on its own terms rather than becoming a colony. The Meiji leaders, having watched China humiliated in the Opium Wars, concluded that Japan must adopt Western military and industrial technology while preserving Japanese identity, a program summed up in the slogan 'rich country, strong army.' Unlike China, where reformers struggled against a vast entrenched bureaucracy and a Manchu court suspicious of change, Japan's new leaders controlled a compact centralized state and could impose conscription, universal education, and land-tax reform by decree. Yet historians also stress the limits of the transformation: the Meiji state was authoritarian, not liberal, and former samurai simply exchanged their swords for bureaucratic office, carrying old hierarchies into the new order.
—Historian's account of modernization in Japan in the period c. 1750–1900

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE goal stated in the Charter Oath.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which the Charter Oath signaled a break with Tokugawa-era policies.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why the Meiji leaders issued the Charter Oath in 1868.

sample_answers.a: The Oath promises that 'knowledge shall be sought throughout the world,' committing Japan to learning from foreign countries in order to strengthen the nation.
sample_answers.b: The pledge to break with 'evil customs of the past' and to let all classes pursue their own callings rejected the Tokugawa rigid four-class hierarchy and the policy of national seclusion.
sample_answers.c: The new leaders needed to legitimize their seizure of power from the Tokugawa shogunate and rally the Japanese people behind a program of rapid reform; the Oath, issued in the emperor's name, gave modernization sacred imperial authority.

q2.stimulus:
Deliberative assemblies shall be widely established and all matters decided by public discussion. All classes, high and low, shall unite in vigorously carrying out the administration of affairs of state. Evil customs of the past shall be broken off and everything based upon the just laws of Nature. Knowledge shall be sought throughout the world so as to strengthen the foundations of imperial rule.
—Charter Oath of the Meiji Emperor, 1868

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the scroll painting that shows the Japanese perspective on the Americans.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which the arrival of Perry's 'black ships' caused political change in Japan.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between Japan's response to Perry's expedition and China's response to Western pressure in the same period.

sample_answers.a: The Japanese artist depicts the American commander with careful attention to his foreign uniform, weapons, and physical features, presenting the Americans as exotic and formidable outsiders to be studied — reflecting Japanese curiosity mixed with alarm.
sample_answers.b: Perry's forced opening of Japan discredited the Tokugawa shogunate, which had failed to repel the foreigners; samurai from outlying domains used the slogan 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarian' to overthrow the shogunate and launch the Meiji Restoration.
sample_answers.c: Japan's leaders responded to Western pressure by centralizing power and deliberately adopting Western technology and institutions, while China's Qing government resisted fundamental reform, leaving China vulnerable to further foreign encroachment and internal rebellion.

q3.stimulus: The image is from the Black Ship Scroll, a Japanese painted scroll from 1854 depicting the arrival of Commodore Matthew Perry's American naval squadron — the 'black ships' — at Uraga Bay in 1853–54. The scroll shows American officers, sailors, and their steam warships as seen through Japanese eyes. Perry's expedition forced Japan to end over two centuries of seclusion and sign the Treaty of Kanagawa (1854), opening Japanese ports to American ships.
